claims.text: The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles have a uniform, well-mixed elemental composition.
Differential element diffusion occurs during heating of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Differential diffusion promotes preferential surface segregation of Cu and portions of Ni.
Cu and the relevant segregating elements have lower surface energy than the other constituents.
Surface segregation produces compositionally distinct, Cu-enriched surface domains.
Segregation of lower-surface-energy elements locally reduces cohesive energy.
Reduced local cohesive energy lowers the local melting point.
Locally lowered melting points cause melting to initiate heterogeneously at the nanoparticle surface and spread inward.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will begin surface melting earlier than comparable binary Ni–Co nanoparticles.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will exhibit a broader premelting temperature interval than the binary baseline.
Locations that melt first will spatially correlate with Cu-enriched or similarly segregated regions.
Slower heating ramps will permit more diffusion and segregation than faster ramps.
The extent or pattern of premelting will depend on heating rate.
Comparable binary Ni–Co nanoparticles lack substantial segregation.
Comparable binary Ni–Co nanoparticles exhibit a uniform, approximately single-step melting transition with minimal premelting.
The proposed comparison varies heating rate between approximately 1 K/s and 10 K/s while controlling particle size and beam-induced effects.
The proposed temperature program covers approximately 0.7Tm to 1.1Tm in increments of about 10 K under high vacuum.
The hypothesized behavior may not apply to substantially different particle sizes or to environments that introduce additional phase interactions.
